title: Fox Bets Big on Creator Freedom, Inking Deals with Josh Richards, Emelia Hartford, and More
summary: In a bold move that flips the traditional Hollywood power dynamic, Fox Creator Studios is expanding its roster with seven new digital-native creators — and promising them something almost unheard of: total creative freedom. The new signees include Canadian influencer Josh Richards, racing personality Emelia Hartford, the trio behind Speeed Co, food creators Sorted Food and MyHealthyDish, Christina Richardson’s microseries franchise, and Alice Ma’s Mad Realities company. Together, they command a combined social footprint of 65 million followers. They join established names like Gordon Ramsay and Tom Segura on the studio’s slate. Billy Parks, head of Fox Creator Studios, told Variety the goal is to create “long-lasting, durable” intellectual property by backing creators who are already deeply connected to their audiences. “We want to show up for different sizes of creators, different types of content and different formats,” Parks said. The deals are structured in a way that’s rare for a major media company: Fox finances the productions and takes a stake in the IP, but retains no final cut. “We don’t give notes,” Parks emphasized. “If they invite us into the creative process, we’re happy to do it, but generally we like to get behind projects that they are excited about.” The slate includes Richards’ sketch comedy show “Read the Room,” which will get two more seasons co-produced with his CrossCheck studio, and Hartford’s “Hot Laps,” a celebrity interview series filmed on race tracks. Parks declined to reveal which celebrities are booked, but the concept — putting stars in high-performance cars for authentic conversations — is designed to capture the magic of people “completely out of their element.” The expansion comes six months after Fox launched the creator-focused arm, and just as the company announced a $22 billion acquisition of Roku. Parks hinted at future synergies but stayed mum on details. He did, however, leave the door wide open for creators using AI tools. “If it’s a good story, well told, we’re here,” he said. For a legacy network navigating the decline of linear TV, this creator-first approach isn’t just a gamble — it’s a blueprint for the future of entertainment.
why_it_matters: This deal signals a massive shift in who gets to make TV and movies: the internet generation now holds the bargaining power once reserved for Hollywood elite. If this model works, future entertainment could be less about big studio committees and more about the voices you already follow on your phone—reshaping what it means to have a ‘real’ career in media.

background_read: Fox Corporation is the broadcaster behind Fox News, Fox Sports, and the Fox network, one of the four legacy U.S. television networks that once dominated American living rooms. For decades, TV studios kept tight control over content, with executives giving ‘notes’ (demands for changes) before a show could air.

The rise of YouTube, Twitch, and TikTok created a parallel entertainment industry where creators like Josh Richards (a Canadian influencer with millions of followers on Vine and later TikTok) can reach audiences without any studio gatekeeper. This made ‘creator economy’ a buzzword as brands and media companies scrambled to tap digital-native stars.

Roku, a company that makes streaming devices and runs a popular ad-supported streaming platform, was acquired by Fox in a deal that signals the network’s ambition to merge traditional television with large-scale digital distribution. The move mirrors other mergers like Disney’s purchase of the majority of 21st Century Fox—but here, Fox is the one buying rather than selling.

perspectives.description: Fox’s approach could open doors for diverse storytellers who wouldn’t survive a traditional notes-heavy system. Retaining creative freedom while getting studio funding lets creators take risks and build lasting IP they partly own—a win for artistic vision and business.

A major network financing shows with no oversight can also mean less protection for quality; a bad project could damage a creator’s brand. Fox taking a stake in the IP while claiming to offer total freedom may mask a long-term power imbalance if those stakes turn into veto rights later.

This is part of a larger pattern: legacy media desperately needs younger audiences, and digital creators need resources to scale. The same shift happened when streaming services lured established TV stars with ‘creative control.’ Now it’s the other way around—studios chase the influencers. The outcome depends on how well these partnerships balance trust and accountability.

If AI-generated scripts and deepfake avatars become common, Fox’s openness to AI tools might let creators produce more for less, but could also flood platforms with low-effort content. The real test is whether these shows can build lasting fanbases, and if the Roku acquisition becomes a distribution pipeline that bypasses traditional networks entirely.
